body_markdown:
The pale blue Mercedes sits at the starting line; its owner, Jim Siegel, eagerly anticipates the green flag. Plenty of models that wear the three-pointed star enjoy rich racing histories, but it’s safe to say that this specific 280SL is in a class of its own at the Bellefontaine Hill Climb Revival near Zanesfield, Ohio.


“Jim brings a lot of fun to the Hill Climb, a perennial frontrunner in the ‘Whitewall Class’ with the 280SL,” says Kurt Niemeyer, one of the event organizers, joking about Jim’s choice to install whitewall tires as an homage to how his dad ordered the car.


Jim set to conquer Corkscrew Hill.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


Indeed, those whitewalls are indicative of the more leisurely pace that the ’69 Mercedes-Benz 280SL would have been accustomed to when Jim’s dad, Dr. Paul Siegel, DDS, was commuting behind the wheel. Jim has fond memories of jaunts with his dad, especially the long road trips. “We would vacation in Northern Michigan every summer,” says Jim, whose family hails from Cincinnati, Ohio. “Dad had the SL up there in the early ’70s and then a couple of times in the ’80s.”


The 500-mile trips from Jim’s Cinci home to Harbor Springs were the longest for the German convertible, going back to when his dad bought the car new in September 1968. Dr. Siegel died in 2003, and Jim bought the SL out of the estate two years later. Under Jim’s stewardship, the Merc gets a thousand or so miles a year, with quite a few of them at speed.


Dr. Paul Siegel in Harbor Springs, Michigan, circa 1986.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


These days, the longest trip the SL takes is the 100-mile drive to Corkscrew Hill near Zanesfield to compete in the Bellefontaine Hill Climb Revival. Originally run from 1953-1974, the event returned in 2019 after local enthusiasts Kurt Niemeyer and Tom Cole formed Sports Car Preservation, Ltd. to revive it. On August 22, Jim ran the eighth event in the SL, and his son John won the 2.5-liter class in his Porsche 944S. Son Mike, an aviation company dispatcher, flew his dad and brother over the course in a Piper Cherokee to check it out before the competition.


Jim deftly manages the 280SL’s swing-axle handling quirks in the high-speed runs.


Scott E. Zimmermann


“The classes are usually small, maybe three cars,” Jim says. “If I run into a 240Z or Austin-Healey, I’m not going to beat those cars, because they’re much lighter than the SL. Any events that I do in this car, I drive it there. I never trailer it. I haven’t broken anything competing.”


The Hill Climb revival’s founder jokes that Jim leads the “Whitewall Class” thanks to running whitewall tires, as the car was ordered new.


Scott E. Zimmermann


## Buying the 280SL


There was already a Mercedes sports car in the Siegel family when Jim was born in 1964. Replacing a 1956 Thunderbird, his dad and mom, Ann Siegel, ordered a 1959 190SL through Shepphards Service in Cincinnati and selected the brand’s European Delivery option.


Dr. Siegel with his children in his 190SL in 1962, two years before Jim was born.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


“They called the trip a second honeymoon and took delivery in Switzerland to drive around Europe,” Jim says. “Dad admired and enjoyed fine and high quality, and he found that in the Mercedes \[190SL\].”


Dr. Siegel worked with high-precision tools as an endodontist, which specializes in root canals. Jim’s grandfather, Dr. Rudolph Siegel, was a pioneer in that field. Jim said his father was more of an airplane enthusiast than a car buff. He restored and flew a 1947 Aeronca Champ and flew model airplanes, too.


Jim’s brother Rudy at the wheel of the 280SL around 1971, posing with the 1947 Aeronca Champ their father restored and flew.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


Though he might’ve been more into planes than cars, Dr. Siegel evidently appreciated Mercedes convertibles enough to buy a second one a decade after his first. He ordered the 280SL with the no-extra-cost four-speed manual, which was rare; most had the four-speed automatic. Other options he chose included:


- Power steering: $200
- Becker Europa AM/FM radio: $174
- Tinted glass: $43
- Whitewall tires: $46


Courtesy Jim Siegel


The 280SL’s price came to $7558 even, including a $71 credit for omitting front-seat headrests. Those would become mandatory on U.S.-market cars starting in January 1969, a few months after Dr. Siegel took delivery.


Luxurious though the little Benz may have been, not all the boxes got ticked. “Dad didn’t feel he needed air conditioning,” Jim said. “He had a 15-minute commute, and he kept the car in a garage at home. When he got to his office, he parked in a below-ground garage.”


The ’69 280SL with four-speed and no A/C cost nearly $7600 in fall 1968, about $75,000 today.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


When the 280SL arrived in Cincinnati, four-year-old Jim accompanied him to the dealership. Jim’s father and oldest brother, Paul Jr., then restored and repainted the red 190SL in the basement garage.


Jim’s father, Dr. Paul Siegel, with his 1959 190SL and 1969 280SL.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


“The car had rust from the salt they used on Cincinnati roads,” Jim said. “Paul then drove it through college and dental school. After my parents passed away, one of my sisters bought the 190, but she sold it two years later.”


Arthritis forced Dr. Siegel to retire in 1979. He kept driving the 280SL, which had suffered the same rusted-fender fate as the 190, though the tin worm spared the 280’s aluminum hood, trunk lid, and door skins. In 1980, he had Tom Justice of Valley Paint and Body in Amelia, Ohio, replace the four fenders and repaint the body in its original Horizon Blue.


“From then on, it was Dad’s weekend fun car,” Jim said. “He taught me to drive a stick shift with the 280SL. He’d tell me to shift so that my passenger couldn’t feel the shifting.”


That was easier said than done, as Jim remembers that the four-speed’s short gearing made the car react jerkily when shifting.


Jim’s mom, Ann, shows off the brand-new 280SL in fall 1968.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


After graduating college in 1986, Jim returned to the dealership where his father bought the SL, this time for a job. He sold Mercedes for nine years. It was a good gig, but the hours were not family-friendly. Jim left to work for Anthem Blue Cross in the phone enrollment department.


## Factory Basics: Mercedes-Benz 280SL


For 1963, Mercedes replaced both the high-end 300SL Roadster and its lower-priced, four-cylinder 190SL sibling with something in between. The 230SL was the first model in the[W113 series designed by Paul Bracq](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/60-years-on-the-mercedes-sl-pagoda-remains-a-masterclass-in-car-design/) , head of Mercedes design. This second-gen SL was less expensive and easier to live with than the exotic 300SL, while offering big leaps in performance and comfort over the 190SL.


The W113’s detachable hardtop, with its lower center section, gave this SL series its “Pagoda” nickname. The unusual roof design feature was not for aesthetics; it came from the mind of influential Mercedes safety engineer, Béla Barényi, as a means of enhancing rollover strength.


The inline-six is all original except for regular maintenance by a vintage Mercedes specialist.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


The 230SL badge signified the car’s 2.3-liter SOHC inline-six with mechanical fuel injection. Its 150 horsepower seemed tame compared to the Jaguar E-Type’s 265 hp but was far more than available in a Porsche 356. The 230SL, however, weighed about 300 pounds more than the Jaguar and 900 more than the Porsche. A 10-second zero-to-60 time put the 230SL in league with the much less expensive Triumph TR4. The Mercedes, though, was more of a grand-touring convertible than a purist roadster.


An improved 2.5-liter six arrived with the 250SL in 1966, followed two years later by the 180-hp, 2.8-liter 280SL. Mercedes made some suspension improvements and eventually offered a five-speed stick, which remained rare. An automatic 280SL could find 60 mph in about 9 seconds, with the stick-shift car perhaps a few ticks quicker. Swing-axle rear suspension could yield tricky handling behavior amid fast cornering, though few SL drivers likely pushed their cars to those limits. The 280SL was the best-selling W113, with 24,000 sold in the U.S. over four years.


## A Cared-for Original


The SL’s cabin is all-original except for replacement seatbelts and one panel on the driver’s seat.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


In his final years, Dr. Siegel had to stop driving his SL. Jim would take it out occasionally to keep the battery charged and circulate the fluids. When he went to collect the car after buying it in 2005, his eight-year-old son, John, accompanied him. John later told his father that the memory of watching him pull the cover off the car and then starting it triggered his interest in cars. He’s now a features engineer for Ford Racing, where one of his projects is working on launch-control systems, and he’s helped with a thing or two on the 280, including installing a new master cylinder. “It took him under an hour,” Jim says.


Jim’s car-buff sons, John and Mike, in 2013. The car inspired John to pursue a career in automotive engineering.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


Aside from the 280SL’s fender replacement and repaint, Jim says the car remains mostly original. The powertrain has never been rebuilt. The original MB-Tex vinyl interior has held up well, with just one worn panel on the driver’s seat replaced. Jim had the ventilation system levers changed out a few years ago. There are no mechanical or cosmetic modifications to the car.


“I haven’t cut holes to put speakers in it or anything like that. The clock still works and is accurate,” he said. “I’ve had the seatbelts replaced but kept the original latches, which are kind of weird, like two interlocking loops. They confuse people, and I have to show them how they work.”


The car’s original Becker Europa radio still plays tunes, though Jim prefers to just listen to the car.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


Jim takes his 280 to Mercedes specialist Precision Motorcars, a shop his father began using in 1972 after the dealer could not fix a drivability issue to his satisfaction. The shop changed hands about 20 years ago and is now owned by Tyler Winslow. He says they’ve gotten the car running beautifully.


Though Precision handles most of the work, Jim and his family have performed a maintenance item or two in the past. He recalls replacing the car’s heater core while the car was still in his dad’s hands. “I was crumpled up in the footwell with Dad walking me through the instructions,” he said. “It was a difficult job. That’s when I realized that working on cars was not something I wanted to do. When I got the core out, he looked at it and got excited. He said, ‘Look at this aluminum washer. It was cut to this size just for this car.’ He was really into details like that.”


Jim’s dad ordered the 280SL via the Mercedes-Benz European Delivery program.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


Jim says the SL is a comfortable ride, he said, but a little loud. But when the mechanic told him the muffler’s baffles were shot, Jim passed on replacing it, not wanting to go the other way and have it be too quiet.


“It’s got a sweet exhaust note, especially from 3000-4000 rpm. At highway speeds, you’re running about 4000 rpm, but the engine’s made to do that.”


The 280SL in Harbor Springs, Michigan, around 2013.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


Jim lent his treasured SL for his niece’s wedding. The groom had learned to drive stick-shift just for the occasion.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


The SL gets its share of more docile driving, too. Jim’s niece used the convertible for her wedding, with the groom getting a quick course in driving a stick-shift from the bride’s dad. “He managed to leave the wedding without stalling,” Jim said. “I had wanted to use it in my own wedding, but the day we got married in September 1989, it was 95 degrees and thunderstorms the whole day.”


Jim often joins his brother, Paul, a Porsche enthusiast, at the local Cars & Coffee and on road tours with Paul’s cohorts. The SL gained some fame when an ad agency featured it in an internet commercial for a local insurance agency. Jim used the fee he received to buy a new soft top for the car.


Jim rented out his SL for a local insurance agency’s commercial and used the money to buy a new soft top.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


It’s seen just about every kind of duty that a Pagoda Merc can, and there’s no doubt that Dr. Siegel’s 280SL has spread joy across generations. Whether for whipping up hillclimbs or heading out for a cruise with his wife, Martha, Jim isn’t letting go. “I plan to keep the 280SL for the rest of my life.”


Jim Siegel and his wife, Martha, with the 280SL in 2013.


Courtesy Jim Siegel


***


**Car:** 1969 Mercedes-Benz 280SL


**Name:** Jim Siegel


**Home:** Cincinnati, Ohio


**Delivery date:** September, 1968


**Miles on car:** 113,400
